questions.q: Which triad defines diabetic ketoacidosis?
ch: Hyperglycemia, ketosis and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
Hyperglycemia, hypernatremia and respiratory alkalosis
Hypoglycemia, ketosis and metabolic alkalosis
Hyperglycemia, hyperkalemia and normal anion gap
Hyperosmolality, minimal ketones and a normal pH
questions.exp: DKA is defined by the triad of hyperglycemia, ketosis and a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, driven by insulin deficiency with lipolysis and ketone production.
why: Hypernatremia and alkalosis are not features of DKA.
Glucose is elevated, not low, and the disturbance is an acidosis.
The acidosis in DKA is high anion gap, not normal gap.
Hyperosmolality with minimal ketones and a normal pH describes HHS, not DKA.

questions.q: Which mnemonic captures the common precipitants of DKA?
ch: The 5 F's: fat, fluid, flatus, faeces and fetus
The 5 I's: infection, insulin omission, ischemia, intoxication, iatrogenic
The 6 P's: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia
The 4 T's: trauma, tumour, thyroid disease, transfusion
The 3 C's: cough, cyanosis and clubbing
questions.exp: The 5 I's: Infection, Insulin deficiency or missed doses, Ischemia or infarction, Intoxication, and Iatrogenic causes. New-onset type 1 diabetes is also a common presentation.
why: The 5 F's describe causes of abdominal distension, not DKA.
The 6 P's describe acute limb ischemia.
The 4 T's describe causes of an anterior mediastinal mass.
The 3 C's are not a DKA mnemonic.

questions.q: What is the first treatment priority in DKA?
ch: Oral rehydration with a glucose solution
Intravenous insulin infusion
Intravenous isotonic fluid to restore volume
Sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis
Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin
questions.exp: Restoring volume with isotonic fluid is the first priority. Osmotic diuresis has caused profound dehydration, and fluids are corrected before or alongside insulin.
why: Oral rehydration is inadequate and glucose would worsen the hyperglycemia.
Insulin follows fluid and potassium; it is not the first step.
Bicarbonate is reserved for severe acidosis with a pH below 6.9 and is not routine.
The subcutaneous route is unreliable in a dehydrated, acidotic patient.

questions.q: A patient in DKA has a serum potassium of 3.0 mmol/L. What must be done?
ch: Proceed with the standard insulin infusion
Give a potassium-binding resin before insulin
Start the insulin infusion at a reduced rate
Hold insulin until potassium is repleted
Give insulin together with sodium bicarbonate
questions.exp: Insulin must be held until potassium is repleted if it is below 3.3 mmol/L. Insulin drives potassium into cells and giving it to a hypokalemic patient can precipitate a fatal arrhythmia.
why: Standard infusion in a hypokalemic patient is exactly the lethal error.
A binding resin lowers potassium further, the opposite of what is needed.
Reducing the rate does not remove the arrhythmia risk; insulin must be held.
Bicarbonate lowers potassium further and compounds the danger.

questions.q: Why can the serum potassium look normal or high at presentation in DKA?
ch: Because total body potassium stores are genuinely elevated in ketoacidosis
Because the failing kidney retains potassium throughout the acidotic period
Because circulating ketone bodies falsely raise the measured potassium value
Because dehydration reduces renal potassium excretion to essentially zero
Because acidosis and insulin deficiency shift potassium out of cells despite a total-body deficit
questions.exp: Total body potassium is depleted even when the serum value looks normal or high, because acidosis and insulin deficiency shift potassium extracellularly. It will plummet once treatment begins.
why: Total body potassium is depleted, not elevated.
Osmotic diuresis causes renal potassium loss rather than retention.
Ketones do not interfere with the potassium assay.
Excretion is increased by the osmotic diuresis, not abolished.

questions.q: When should the intravenous insulin infusion be stopped in DKA?
ch: Once the anion gap has closed
After the first litre of fluid has been given
When urinary ketones first become negative
After a fixed period of six hours
As soon as the glucose falls below 200 mg/dL
questions.exp: Treat the gap, not the glucose. Insulin continues, with dextrose added to the fluid as glucose falls, until the anion gap closes.
why: Fluid volume is not the endpoint for insulin.
Urine ketones lag and reflect acetoacetate rather than beta-hydroxybutyrate.
A fixed duration ignores the patient's biochemistry.
Glucose normalises before ketogenesis stops; stopping here leaves the patient acidotic.

questions.q: Why must subcutaneous insulin overlap with the intravenous infusion before it is stopped?
ch: Because the overlap period allows potassium to redistribute safely
Because intravenous insulin has a very short half-life and ketosis rebounds after an unbridged stop
Because the subcutaneous dose would otherwise cause profound hypoglycemia
Because overlapping the two routes reduces the total daily insulin requirement
Because subcutaneous insulin reaches peak effect within a few seconds
questions.exp: Intravenous insulin has a very short half-life. Subcutaneous insulin must be given 1 to 2 hours before the drip is stopped, or ketosis rebounds in the gap.
why: Potassium shifts are managed by replacement and monitoring, not by the overlap.
The risk of an unbridged stop is rebound ketosis, not hypoglycemia.
Overlap is about continuity of insulin effect, not total dose.
Subcutaneous insulin takes time to act, which is precisely why overlap is needed.

questions.q: A child being treated for DKA develops headache and deteriorating consciousness. What should be suspected?
ch: Resolution of the acidosis
Rebound hyperglycemia
Cerebral edema
Hypoglycemia from excess insulin
An unrelated migraine
questions.exp: Headache and deteriorating mentation in a child during DKA treatment signals cerebral edema, an emergency.
why: Resolution improves rather than depresses consciousness.
Rebound hyperglycemia does not cause acute deterioration in consciousness.
Hypoglycemia is possible and should be checked, but this specific pattern in a child is the classic warning of cerebral edema.
Attributing new neurological deterioration to migraine risks missing a lethal complication.

questions.q: An acidotic patient with type 2 diabetes on an SGLT2 inhibitor has a glucose of 180 mg/dL. What should be considered?
ch: Simple starvation ketosis
A laboratory error in the glucose measurement
Lactic acidosis from metformin
Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
questions.exp: Think euglycemic DKA in an acidotic diabetic on an SGLT2 inhibitor whose glucose is deceptively normal. The ketoacidosis is present despite the unremarkable glucose.
why: Starvation ketosis does not usually produce a severe high-gap acidosis in this context.
Dismissing the glucose as an error misses a recognised and dangerous presentation.
Metformin-associated lactic acidosis is rare and would not produce ketosis.
HHS is defined by marked hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality with minimal ketones.

questions.q: A patient with DKA remains acidotic despite appropriate fluids, insulin and potassium replacement. What should be considered?
ch: That bicarbonate should be given routinely
That the diagnosis must be HHS instead
That treatment should be stopped and restarted
That the anion gap is an unreliable measure
Ongoing sepsis or ischemia, or inadequate insulin and fluid delivery
questions.exp: Persistent acidosis despite treatment points to an ongoing precipitant such as sepsis or ischemia, or to inadequate insulin and fluid delivery. Search for the precipitant.
why: Bicarbonate is reserved for a pH below 6.9 and does not address the cause.
HHS is characterised by minimal ketones and would not explain persistent ketoacidosis.
Interrupting treatment worsens the acidosis.
The anion gap is the standard measure used to track resolution.

questions.q: Which pair of abnormalities underlies type 2 diabetes?
ch: Insulin resistance with relative insulin deficiency
Excess glucagon with normal insulin sensitivity
Impaired renal glucose reabsorption alone
Deficient thyroid hormone with slowed metabolism
Autoimmune beta-cell destruction and absolute insulin deficiency
questions.exp: Type 2 diabetes results from insulin resistance plus relative insulin deficiency from progressive beta-cell dysfunction, strongly linked to obesity, inactivity, genetics and metabolic syndrome.
why: Glucagon excess is not the defining mechanism.
Renal glucose handling is not the primary defect.
Thyroid deficiency is an unrelated endocrine disorder.
Autoimmune destruction with absolute deficiency describes type 1 diabetes.

questions.q: Which result establishes a diagnosis of diabetes?
ch: Random glucose of 160 mg/dL without symptoms
Fasting glucose of 110 mg/dL
HbA1c of 6.5% or above
HbA1c of 5.9%
Two-hour OGTT value of 150 mg/dL
questions.exp: Diagnosis requires any of: HbA1c 6.5% or above, fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or above, two-hour OGTT 200 mg/dL or above, or a random glucose of 200 mg/dL or above with symptoms, confirmed on repeat unless unequivocal.
why: A random glucose of 160 is below the threshold and there are no symptoms.
A fasting glucose of 110 falls in the prediabetes range of 100 to 125.
An HbA1c of 5.9% is prediabetes, which spans 5.7 to 6.4%.
A two-hour value of 150 is below the 200 threshold.

questions.q: Which agent is first-line pharmacotherapy for type 2 diabetes?
ch: Sitagliptin
Empagliflozin
Glipizide
Metformin
Insulin glargine
questions.exp: Metformin is first-line, reducing hepatic glucose output. It does not cause hypoglycemia or weight gain.
why: A DPP-4 inhibitor gives modest, weight-neutral benefit and is not first-line.
An SGLT2 inhibitor is preferred where there is CKD or heart failure, but metformin remains first-line.
A sulfonylurea is inexpensive and effective but causes hypoglycemia and weight gain.
Insulin is reserved for when oral agents are insufficient or the A1c is very high.

questions.q: Which agent should be preferred in a patient with type 2 diabetes and heart failure or chronic kidney disease?
ch: A DPP-4 inhibitor
Basal insulin alone
A thiazolidinedione
A sulfonylurea
An SGLT2 inhibitor
questions.exp: SGLT2 inhibitors have cardiovascular, renal and heart-failure benefit and are preferred with CKD or heart failure. With ASCVD or obesity, a GLP-1 receptor agonist is favoured. Choose for organ benefit, not just glucose.
why: DPP-4 inhibitors are weight-neutral but lack the cardiorenal benefit.
Insulin controls glucose without the organ-protective effect.
Thiazolidinediones can worsen fluid retention in heart failure.
Sulfonylureas offer no organ protection and cause hypoglycemia.

questions.q: When should metformin be temporarily withheld?
ch: Around iodinated contrast administration and in acute kidney injury
Before every meal to avoid gastrointestinal upset
During any febrile illness regardless of severity
Whenever the glycated haemoglobin falls below 7%
Before any period of moderate physical exercise
questions.exp: Metformin is held around iodinated contrast and in renal impairment or acute kidney injury, because of the rare risk of lactic acidosis.
why: Metformin is taken with meals to reduce gastrointestinal upset, not withheld.
Fever alone is not an indication to stop metformin.
A good A1c is not a reason to withhold a dose.
Exercise does not require holding metformin.

questions.q: What is the '15-15 rule' for treating hypoglycemia?
ch: 15 units of insulin then recheck in 15 minutes
15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate then recheck in 15 minutes
15 mL of dextrose over 15 seconds
A 15% dextrose infusion for 15 hours
15 minutes of rest then 15 minutes of activity
questions.exp: Give 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck the glucose in 15 minutes.
why: Insulin would deepen the hypoglycemia.
This is not the described rule and the volume is inadequate.
A prolonged infusion is not what the rule describes.
Rest and activity do not treat hypoglycemia.

questions.q: Which complications are classified as microvascular in diabetes?
ch: Coronary artery disease, stroke and peripheral arterial disease
Retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy
Retinopathy, stroke and peripheral arterial disease
Nephropathy, coronary disease and neuropathy
Cataract, gastritis and osteoporosis
questions.exp: Chronic hyperglycemia damages small vessels, producing retinopathy, nephropathy and neuropathy. Coronary disease, stroke and peripheral arterial disease are the macrovascular complications.
why: These three are the macrovascular complications.
Stroke and peripheral arterial disease are macrovascular.
Coronary disease is macrovascular.
These are not the recognised microvascular triad.

questions.q: Which screening assessments should be performed for diabetic complications?
ch: Bone density scanning with thyroid function and parathyroid hormone
Liver ultrasound with serum ferritin and transferrin saturation
Dilated eye exam, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, foot exam, lipids and blood pressure
Echocardiography and carotid ultrasound with annual stress testing
Annual chest radiography with spirometry and arterial blood gas
questions.exp: Complication screening comprises a dilated eye exam, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, foot exam with monofilament, lipids and blood pressure.
why: These are not the recommended diabetes complication screens.
These do not address the microvascular and macrovascular complications.
These assess vascular disease but omit the core screening set.
Respiratory screening is not part of routine diabetes care.

questions.q: Why should blood pressure and lipids be treated as aggressively as glucose in type 2 diabetes?
ch: Because they determine the A1c value
Because they prevent hypoglycemia
Because they are easier to control
Because most of the mortality in diabetes is cardiovascular
Because glucose control has no benefit
questions.exp: Most of the mortality in diabetes is cardiovascular, so blood pressure and lipid control matter as much as glycemic control.
why: Blood pressure and lipids do not determine the A1c.
They have no bearing on hypoglycemia risk.
Ease of control is not the rationale.
Glucose control does have benefit, particularly for microvascular disease.

questions.q: In which situation may the HbA1c be misleading?
ch: In any patient over the age of 60
When the fasting glucose is normal
When the patient is on insulin
In a patient taking metformin
In haemolysis, recent blood loss or iron deficiency
questions.exp: HbA1c can read falsely low with haemolysis or blood loss and falsely high with iron deficiency, so it should be interpreted in context.
why: Age alone does not invalidate the test.
A normal fasting glucose does not make the A1c unreliable.
Insulin therapy does not interfere with the assay.
Metformin does not distort the A1c measurement.
